utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Due to a major failure of our ICT systems, especially the service, if I understand well, we couldn't start at 9.30. We had to wait for quite a while. Since Mr. Mladic had to wait for a long time in the holding cell, he was given an opportunity to return to the UNDU, but he has preferred to stay here, which is highly appreciated by the Chamber, so that we can see whether we can conclude the testimony of Mr. Akashi today. Mr. Tieger, could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't intend -- given the pace of yesterday, I certainly don't intend to -- basically I would think I would use my allotted time, which is the bulk of the next two sessions, so that I have an hour and 15 minutes left. I'm trying to move forward as quickly as I can, but I don't think, unless the pace quickens, it will be appreciably faster than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we have -- as a matter of fact, I think we have two sessions left. We can continue until a little bit after 2.15 this afternoon. But since Mr. Mladic has been waiting for the whole of the morning, we'll have to impose some limits on ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think ... first of all, Mr. Akashi --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- welcome back in this courtroom. Due to a major failure of our ICT system, we couldn't start at 9.30, which we regret very much. We'll try to see whether we can conclude hearing your evidence this morning. Before we start, perhaps unnecessary, but I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. We were just in the midst of a discussion when you entered the courtroom about whether we could conclude, yes or no. Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at you. Is there anything, if Mr. Tieger would use -- I think you said 1 hour and 15 minutes -- 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I was about to say I will certainly look for ways to stream-line as we go, but that's where we stood at the beginning of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how much time you think would you need, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've got approximately 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So we're cutting it close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we would either take two longer sessions, but, of course, Mr. Mladic, because of you, we usually take sessions of one hour, or we should attach a third short session to see whether both options will be considered. Let's first now continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, yesterday you referred to your frequent requests to visit Banja Luka in light of the information you were receiving about ethnic cleansing and violations of human rights, and in that connection, we looked at your code cable of the 7th of April, 1994, referencing one such request. That's P7694. I'd like to jump forward some months later in 1994 to September of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection call up, please, P2048.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now this is a code cable sent by you to Mr. Annan on the 20th of September, 1994 -- oh, I'm sorry. This is -- and it contains a letter to Dr. Karadzic on that same date. And if we could turn the page, please, to page 2, as we see at the bottom of paragraph 1, you continue to raise the problem of human rights abuses in the Banja Luka area, referring to the most recent departure of Muslims who arrived in the -- in Central Bosnia. Is it correct that that's -- that was a further reflection or ongoing reflection of the same problem that you had protested previously? And you'll have to answer audibly, Mr. Ambassador, rather than with a nod of the head.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, it -- would the -- your reference there to the departures of non-Serb population from the area of Banja Luka, is that part of the continuing effort to bring to the attention of Mr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership the ongoing human rights abuses in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, apparently as we see from the letter, Banja Luka was not the only area where that was happening. As you note at the beginning of your letter, you wished to convey your utter dismay at the fact that in the past few days alone, over 2500 Muslim civilians have been forcibly -- forcefully expelled from the area of Bijeljina and Janja. And as you note later, a little bit later, many of them had been expelled and apparently robbed en route by a man named Vojkan. And that was an accurate reflection of the information you were receiving that you sought to bring to the -- to protest --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- to Mr. Karadzic about?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, your letter indicates that just one month before you had also raised the same issue, the issue of forceful expulsions of the non-Serb population, and that Dr. Karadzic had said to you that such expulsions were not in accordance with the policies of the Bosnian Serb authorities. And I think's found in paragraph 2 of your letter. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. In addition, this matter was pressed by Mr. de Mello who met with Dr. Karadzic on the 8th of September --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- in regard to the same problem and received the same assurances from Dr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we kept receiving assurances which were not reflected on the changes on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to look quickly at the reference -- you reference Mr. de Mello's efforts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In that connection can I call up 65 ter 03478.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a code cable dated 9th of September, 1994, from you to Mr. Annan. As we see in paragraph 1, it refers to Mr. Vieira de Mello's travel on the 8th of September to Sarajevo and Pale to re-establish contact with the Bosnian Serb leadership. And if we turn to page 2 and specifically paragraph 6, we see a reference to what you referred to in your letter of September 20th. HCA, and that's Mr. de Mello, then appealed to Karadzic to put an end to the ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka and Bijeljina and to make public his intention to seize the criminal network in accordance with assurances given three weeks earlier to Akashi and himself. It continues to refer to Dr. Karadzic's assurances and representations in respect of those crimes. And it refers again to Vojkan, noting: HCA reiterated our hope that Karadzic would soon allow Akashi and UNPROFOR to verify independently humanitarian conditions in both regions and repeatedly pressed for the arrest of Vojkan, who Karadzic said might be acting under Arkan's instructions, along with members of his gang. I take it that the reference there --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Ambassador, that the reference by Mr. de Mello to the hope that would Karadzic soon allow you and UNPROFOR to verify independently conditions in both regions is another reflection of your ongoing but unsuccessful efforts to gain access to the areas?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a frustrating exercise to keep repeating our strong demands for rectification of the conditions of life in those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger -- yes, Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7698, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, I -- it took me a while to get back to the English channel. It's a pattern now. You're speaking so quickly that the interpreters, French interpreters, get behind and then Mr. Akashi gives you the good example by talking so quietly that the interpreters catch up again. But I'd rather that the interpreters can follow you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your gentle admonition earlier should have been sufficient but this will have its impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to a related document, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up, please, 65 ter 15781.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As it comes up, sir, you'll see that it's a document dated the 15th of September, 1994, from you to Mr. Annan, relating to Mr. de Mello's meeting with Mr. Simic, the vice-prime minister of FRY, and we can see that on the first -- the first page. As we see in paragraph 3, Mr. de Mello briefs Simic on his last meeting in Pale with Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic and it refers to some of the subjects covered. Turning quickly to paragraph 7 on page 2, it reflects that Mr. de Mello explained to Mr. Simic the issue of ethnic cleansing in Banja Luka and Bijeljina than he had met with Dr. Karadzic on that subject or those subjects, and again explains that Dr. Karadzic indicated that he had taken steps, initiated investigations particularly on the role of Major Vojkan Djurkovic. However, Mr. de Mello stressed that this was an insufficient response as the cleansing itself was apparently continuing. And that by the time the investigations were over, there would be nobody left to expel. And finally, a reference to your continuing efforts to gain access to Banja Luka. This document, sir, is an accurate reflection of the ongoing efforts to press Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership to end the cleansing in those areas?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was one clear proof of our continuing efforts and our failure to get any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7699, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 31392, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, as this document comes up, you will see, as the Chamber and parties will, that it's a report on morale from the East Bosnia Corps command dated the 2nd of October, 1994. And if we turn to page 2, paragraph 1.5, we see a reference to the following: "Since some Muslims moved out of Bijeljina and Janja, a number of residential units were obtained for the needs of IBK soldiers and officers, which affected morale positively." And in the context of the information you had at the time and the matters with which you were dealing, is that a reference, as you understand it, to the departures of Muslims and the expulsions that you and Dr. de Mello had met with Dr. Karadzic about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object to the question. Misstates the document. If you read the next line you'll see what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, does this cause you to read more or to phrase your question differently?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't find those references mutually exclusive, and I think it's up to the Chamber to decide and it's up to the witness to answer. In fact, it refers not to the people who fled but to the people who filled those accommodations. But in any event, I think it's up to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe -- I don't know how else you can interpret a large number of soldiers who had fled. Those are precisely people who had fled, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Found permanent accommodation in Bijeljina and Janja."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. The matter may be revisited during re-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, the question is simply whether that is a reference, as you would understand it, to the ongoing issue of Muslim departure from those -- the areas of Bijeljina and Janja.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I -- I think reference is precisely to the ongoing phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7700, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just one more question about the question of housing and Muslim departure. If I could have 65 ter 02382, please, pages 161 in the English and 168 in the B/C/S. And as I read the English, we'll have to move quickly to 169 in the B/C/S. 161 in the English. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly conducted in September of 1993 and speaking is Mr. Srdic, a delegate from the Krajina region from Prijedor, who says the following: "Gentlemen, think about this thoroughly. This is just the mask Federations of veterans and families of killed soldiers. We have the opportunities to see there have been no families of killed soldiers who have not solved housing problem. There are some of them, but they have not done what they have [sic] been asked. They should have cleansed their municipalities as we had done, and they would have not had any problems [sic]. If any agreement was made, if somebody came back, we would say that many people have been in municipality. You, that had done the job, take the responsibility as the war criminals."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: None of this is in the Serbian. I think it's in the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tried to indicate earlier that we'd need to switch. I'm sorry, I didn't signal as we were going.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tieger speak more slowly, especially when reading, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, it's not the first time today. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it would always be good to give a clear reference where you are reading from, especially for the interpreters. It's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That concludes the passage I wanted to raise. Assuming we've had enough opportunity to see the B/C/S at the top of the next page, I wanted to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, in your discussions with Dr. Karadzic when he offered repeated assurances to your protests, did he tell you about any link being drawn by RS officials, by Republika Srpska officials, between the departures of Muslims, between the cleansings, and the availability of housing for Serb soldiers or Serbs generally?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not specifically recall discussion on that linkage between the two phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank, you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I would tender this excerpt, Mr. President. It should be added to P2508.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it is -- we'll then finalize that later in -- because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's an ongoing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- ongoing exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The portion you read is admitted as such in P2508.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, in the last paragraph of your September 20th letter that we looked at earlier, you stated to Dr. Karadzic that you could not understand how such a deplorable situation could continue and even accelerate despite all the commitments repeatedly made to stop the forcible expulsions. And in that connection, I'd like to show you a transcript of a meeting at which the -- at which Vojkan was discussed and at which the policy of the Bosnian Serb leadership was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I have called up, please, P6723.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, we're looking now at a transcript from the 14th Session of the Supreme Command held on the 31st of March, 1995, or at least a portion of that. And if we could turn just for the -- this begins at pages 3 and 4 with a discussion about convoy of Muslims and Croats. But the pertinent section I wish to particularly bring to your attention begins at the top of page 6 in the English and on page 6 of the B/C/S with Dr. Karadzic speaking. And he begins with saying: "Let me first say something. This is what it is, Srdja Srdic keeps pestering us that this should be done by his CK, Red Cross, that state agencies, et cetera, should do it." So that's another reference to the individual we -- who was speaking at the Bosnian Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think we need the prior page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic continues: "Muslims remaining there in any way is disastrous for us." And he goes on to explain his view of why. After mentioning numbers in respect of Muslims and the Serbs in the areas of the Krajina, that is, Kljuc, Sanski Most, Banja Luka, he continues: "It is the standpoint of our policy there has been a separation of peoples, of cultures, of worlds, birds of a feather flock together ..." Now that reference to the policy and the separation of peoples, of cultures, of worlds, is not dissimilar, I take it, Mr. Ambassador, to what Dr. Karadzic told you about good fences making good neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the question. If he's going to quote from a document verbatim, he should quote verbatim and finish the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're again invited to read more slowly. Especially the French interpreters are not able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll read it -- I could have done it two ways. Let me finish the sentence and ask the two questions I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If do you it all slowly then everything will be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I read the entire relevant portions: "It the standpoint of our policy there has been a separation of peoples, of culture, of worlds, birds of a feather flock together, what Vojkan did is not allowed, for Vojkan to work illegally. He was excluded from the state commission, et cetera. What do private agencies do, they find probably for big money, they secure him a foreign visa and secure him a passport to travel to that foreign country. What happens now, if that were done by a state institution, we would be accused of ethnic cleansing." And then if we turn to page 66 of the English -- excuse me, page 7 of the e-court, 66 in the hard copy, and still page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can't find it in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's page 7 of the B/C/S, precisely in the middle of the page. I'll read it. It's the next portion of Dr. Karadzic speaking after -- he is listed as speaking twice after General Mladic has spoken. And the quote is: "That is why we, because we turn a blind eye at a private agency which makes these private arrangements. When a private" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where are you reading, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm reading from the top of page 7 in the English and the middle of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't see it in either language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. We have page 7 of the English, please, scroll down. "For them have UNPROFOR guard them," the first paragraph. And in the second -- second sentence of that first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have that and you started reading as: "That is why we ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is why we, because we turn a blind eye at a private agency which makes these private arrangements. When a private Muslim and a private agency make arrangements for him to go to Germany, no one can accuse us."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My question for you, Mr. Ambassador, is: During the course of these repeated representations about the actions he was allegedly taking with respect to what Vojkan was doing, did he ever tell you that he turned a blind eye to what Vojkan and others like him were doing because of his view that it insulated the Bosnian Serb leadership from being accused of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object to the question. It takes the matter out of context and the remainder of the first part that was not read illuminates this matter greatly, I think. The Prosecutor is misrepresenting the text of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall specific reference to -- to the -- to the matter you have just drawn my attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Contrary to turning a -- contrary to the -- let me put it this way. What Dr. Karadzic told you was he was actively investigating and seeking to arrest and punish Vojkan, not turning a blind eye to his activities; right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that specific discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'd like to turn to one more example of the representations that were made to you by Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership that were not fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection can we turn, please, to 65 ter 30739.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is a weekly report from the 24th through the 31st of July, 1995, from the UNPROFOR HQ Sarajevo. It has a section beginning on page 3 of the English, page 4 -- it says -- actually page 4 of the e-court on Srebrenica and Zepa. You see the discussion begins there, referring to some of the events that had taken place up to that point. And then it continues on to the next page, page 5, at the bottom of the first paragraph of page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, no B/C/S translation available?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I'll read slowly and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And take care that everything is well in context and take care that the -- if you want to tender it later, that a translation be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely why I showed where the subject began in the report and where it is related to the quote I'm bringing to the Ambassador's attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the bottom of that first paragraph, it states: "The persistent refusal of the Serb side to provide a list of the prisoners held after the fall of Srebrenica, the alleged killing in Zepa, even after negotiations, of the ABiH commander Avdo Palic, and the announced intention of the Serbs of trying other 'war criminals' seemed to justify anxieties." Now, that reference to the persistent refusal of the Serb side to provide a list of prisoners is a reflection, is it not, Mr. Ambassador, of pressure from the international community to get access to people who had been taken prisoner and of concern about their fate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you -- could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. With respect to the reference there to the persistent refusal of the Serb side to provide a list of prisoners, that reflects, does it not, ongoing efforts and pressure by the international community to get access to people who had been taken prisoner and reflects concern about their fate; is that right? Or to put it another way, I presume that refusal -- the reference to refusal is in context a reference to requests that were unfulfilled?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender the document, Mr. President, 30739. And I know it needs a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7701, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can take the next two documents together, Mr. Ambassador, since they appear to be related. The first one is 65 ter 03544. And this is an outgoing code cable from you to Mr. Annan dated the 14th of August, 1995, in reference to the missing population from Srebrenica. And on page 2, we see a letter to Dr. Karadzic which was attached, in which you express concern about the reports of grave violations of international humanitarian law in and around Srebrenica, and, among other things, request immediate access for representatives of UNHCR, the ICRC, et cetera, to persons displaced, and further that you permit representatives to visit and register any persons detained against their will. And I said I want to take two documents because I thought they were related.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could also call up 13311.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And this is an outgoing code cable dated the 22nd of August, 1995, which refers, among other things, as we see from the top -- from the first page, to meetings with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including Dr. Karadzic, on the 21st of August. And I believe these are meetings by the chief of mission, Mr. Ambassador, not yourself. If we turn to page 3, there's a reference to the discussion regarding Srebrenica at that meeting, noting: I reminded Karadzic that accordance with the directives of UN Resolution 1010, concerning reports of grave violations of international law, the SRSG had written to him on 12 August to request access and cooperation for UNPROFOR to investigate the allegations. To date, the SRSG has not received Karadzic's response, nor had the latter reacted in any positive manner to the request. I urge Karadzic to give urgent consideration to SRSG's request. Karadzic claimed that he had lately been preoccupied with the crisis in Banja Luka and other areas and promised to look into the matter. Those two documents we just looked at, Mr. Ambassador, do those correctly reflect ongoing efforts by yourself and other members of the international community to obtain information about the whereabouts and fate of those persons who had been taken prisoner following the taking of Srebrenica by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger. I think as -- since particularly from the meeting which took place with President Milosevic and others on the Bosnian Serb side with several of us from the UN and from the rest of the international community, we made persistent efforts for them to fulfil their promise, including the visit by ICRC to the areas of Srebrenica to investigate and verify whether the persistent rumours about possible tragedy that has taken place could be confirmed. But these efforts were in vain, efforts on our part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those two documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 03544 will be Exhibit P7702. And 65 ter 13311 will be Exhibit P7703.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: English translations are -- is available for the first one, not for the second one. Is -- the first one, then, yes, they are together in one -- under one number. P7703 will be marked for identification awaiting a translation of a portion of it. Please proceed. And is marked for identification, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. May I have 65 ter 04472, page 89, please. In the -- page 89 in English and page 165 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to wrap up our discussion on this issue, I wanted to draw your attention to the following, Mr. Ambassador. At the bottom of the page, after a discussion in paragraph 408 concerning the reaction of the Special Rapporteur for Human Rights and his concerns about the situation, the blockages of humanitarian aid, the shellings, we see at paragraph 409, the following: "Illustrative of his frustration, ICRC" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we wait until we have 409 on the screen, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Turn the page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Illustrative of his frustration, ICRC had not been granted access to the Srebrenica area to ascertain the fate of" - and if we turn the page, please - "the missing until a few days after the London meeting. Once granted access by the BSA to the Batkovic camp in North-Eastern Bosnia, ICRC was only able to register 164 prisoners from Srebrenica and 44 from Zepa. The ICRC representatives were told that no other prisoners were being held and were accordingly shown a number of empty detention centres in the Bratunac area. As of November 1999," which clearly is a -- that's right. "As of November 1999, 7.336 individuals from Srebrenica remain unaccounted for, based on the number of tracing requests for missing persons received by ICRC." And, Mr. Ambassador, does that reflect what you indicated to us earlier; that is, the efforts -- that is, that the efforts by the international community to repeatedly obtain information about and access to persons who had been taken prisoners remained unsuccessful?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, I think this is part of a -- a great deal of efforts on our part to identify whether all those ominous rumours have the factual basis, and we were still left in a very heavy fog as to what exactly took place in and around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I tender that document, Mr. President. The portion of the document, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You still have to upload because it's now a 113-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you reserve a number for the excerpt still to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be P7704.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then admission will -- even after the uploading will be decided upon once we have B/C/S translation. Oh, it's there. No, I see it's there. The number is reserved for the excerpt to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few other, I think, documents for which no B/C/S translations were provided but we'll deal with that later. And that's both for the Prosecution and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, during the course of your testimony in the Karadzic case, you were asked during cross-examination about a portion in your booklet referring to the detention of UN personnel. That portion -- and I'll read the quote, the question that you were asked and the answer you gave at that time, that occurs at 65 ter 33522, e-court page 29 going onto page 30. "And the question was, at page 31 of the booklet, e-court pages 18 and 19, where you refer to the detention of UN personnel following the NATO air-strikes in May of 1995, and I'd like to know whether you agree with me that UN personnel who were taken hostage on that occasion were used, actually, as human shields in order to compel NATO forces to stop the air-strikes." And your answer was: "I think the term 'human shield' is frequently used by journalism, but in this particular case, I think if we construe Bosnian Serb action of taking UN [sic] personnel as -- as hostage, if this act is construed as taking hostages and making them as human shield is certainly not an exaggeration, journalistic exaggeration." Now, first of all, Mr. Ambassador, that reflects the information provided during the course of the Karadzic case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I just to put -- just to ask you about a contemporaneous expression of that same point, I'd like to turn to 65 ter 33520 which is a code cable dated the 30th of May, 1995. And just to put it somewhat in context, because there was a lot happening that day, we see at paragraph 11 on page 4 of this document reference to the air-strike. And then beginning in the third sentence of that paragraph: "In response, the Serbs surrounded a number of weapon collection points, all safe areas except Zepa were also shelled, resulting in particularly heavy casualties in Tuzla where over 60 civilians were killed and over 130 injured." And then the last sentence of that paragraph: "The Serbs reacted by surrounding additional weapon collection points, taking UNMOs into custody and using a number of them as human shields to deter further air-strikes on potential targets and cutting electricity to the city."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It reads "attacks" rather than "strikes."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. "... to deter further air attacks on potential targets, and cutting electricity to the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I mention it was a cable of the 30th of May and I should have mentioned, Mr. Ambassador, it was from you to Mr. Goulding with information to Mr. Annan and Stoltenberg. Mr. Ambassador, this was a contemporaneous expression of what was happening on the ground and the taking of UN personnel as hostages and human shields to deter air attacks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P7705, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. It's not a very long document, six pages, so I take it that full translation will be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you, Mr. President. I'm trying to adhere to the schedule. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, about the schedule, I'd like to -- we have two options. Either we take a break now, then we would -- that would be a break of 20 minutes. Then we would sit from 1.20 to 2.20. And if that would be agreeable to the Defence, we would then take another break and sit from 20 minutes to 3.00 until 3.30. This would be an overall session not longer than usual, but for the day, of course, since Mr. Mladic arrived at 9.00 in the morning, would be longer. Another option would be to continue for half an hour, then take a break of half an hour, which is a bit of a longer break. That would be from 1.30 to 2.00. And then have a second session from 2.00 to 3.30. The latter option would have the advantage of having three hours overall available, whereas in the first option it would be only two hours and 50 minutes. But we have the short sessions usually in order to accommodate Mr. Mladic. Therefore, I'd like to hear from the Defence whether the option providing a little bit more time, that is, two sessions of one hour and a half with a longer break, would be agreeable to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence, in an effort to accommodate Mr. Akashi who needs to finish today, is agreeable with the second option to sit the longer sessions and have the maximum time to complete the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber certainly appreciates that and I take it that all who are benefiting from this attitude will also appreciate that. Mr. Tieger, you can continue until 1.30 and then you have 20 minutes after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As long as we're on this document, Mr. Ambassador, let me direct your attention, if I might, to paragraph 14. It refers at the last sentence we can see on the page and then moving on to page 5: "There has been a complete breakdown in negotiations to reopen the Sarajevo airport and utilities are again being cut. The problem of resupply in Sarajevo and the eastern enclaves has been further aggravated." Mr. Ambassador, we referred a moment ago to the issue of using UN personnel as human shields to deter air-strikes. Was it also the case that restrictions on humanitarian aid or necessities of life, such as utilities or water, were also used as instrumentalities or weapons of war to -- by the Bosnian Serb authorities to advance objectives?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all these measures taken by the Bosnian Serb side were a means to express their utmost unhappiness about the two air-strikes, one on the 25th and the other on the 27th of May. I tried to remind Mr. Tieger and the others that these were air-strikes as distinct from close air support action, and in this particular instance, the action was taken in full consultation between our Sarajevo headquarters for UNPROFOR Bosnian command and overall headquarters in Zagreb. It was not an isolated ad hoc action, but it was a consequence of deliberate, serious thinking and the reflection on the part of the entire UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me move, if I may, to a different and earlier time-period and an approximately 24- to 36-hour period within that time-frame. If I could first have 65 ter 10106, and I'm going to show you three documents together, I think, in the interests of expediency because they relate to the same matter and almost precisely the same day. They are both from either the 11th or 12th of March. This is a code cable from you to Mr. Annan dated the 12th of March. In the middle of the first paragraph you refer to your arrival back in Sarajevo, and then note, among other things: The closure of the Blue Routes across the Sarajevo airport by the Bosnian Serbs which they say is in response to the killing of the two girls by the shelling last night of down-town Sarajevo with heavy weapons, and by the fact that my aircraft was hit by machine-gun fire as it taxied after landing in Sarajevo. So you refer to those -- among other things, those three aspects of the situation including the closure of the Blue Routes. And again to refresh your memory on that -- or not to refresh, to expand what was happening on that date --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could turn to D461 from March 11th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page -- we'll see the cover page first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska dated the 11th of March, 1995. And if we could turn to page 3 of the document in both the English and the B/C/S, in the middle of the page at point II, under the heading: "Situation in the territory," we see that: "Due to sniper fire and the death of two girls, all [sic] movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys is prohibited until further notice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It reads "any," but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I said "all." "...any movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys is prohibited until further notice."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally another document of the 12th of March related to the same subject, Mr. Ambassador, and that's 65 ter 12003. This is a report the next day from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command to the Main Staff. And if we turn to page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, we see again a report on the situation in the territory which reflects that the order about closing of the Blue Roads has been delivered or issued to the units and it is being implemented in practice. Now, Mr. Ambassador, we had looked earlier at actions taken with respect to utilities and humanitarian supplies in the period of May. Do these documents referring to the closing of the Blue Routes in March also refer to restrictions on humanitarian aid or necessities of life as means of obtaining particular objectives or retaliating?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what is the point of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, we had looked earlier at -- and you had commented on the -- the use of restrictions of aid or necessities of life in the period of May. Now we're looking at one in March of 1995. I simply wanted to ask you if that's another reflection of the same practice.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes, this is part of our efforts to put pressure on the Bosnian government as well as on the efforts, humanitarian efforts, of the United Nations, UNHCR, and all the rest, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I tender 10106 and 12003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be Exhibits P7706 and P7707, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we have translations for both? Yes, we have. P7706 and P7707 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Ambassador, on the specific issue in Sarajevo and the air-strikes and sort of looking at a number of the issues we've just discussed, I wanted to turn your attention to 30743 which is an UNPROFOR weekly sitrep from the week of 28 May 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we can go to -- I just want to canvass this very quickly. If we could go to e-court page 2 and beginning at paragraph 4 in the English and paragraph 4 in the B/C/S as well, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would need the -- paragraph 4 you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we need for both -- at least for the B/C/S the next page, and we start in English at the bottom of this page -- well, the first line was -- but I take it you have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. It begins: "At 1620 hours on 25 May, NATO aircraft conducted an air-strike." It continues by noting the retaliation by the Bosnian Serbs shelling the safe areas of Sarajevo, Bihac, Tuzla, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. It continues by noting that the Serbs raised the ante by taking over 300 UN -- UNPROFOR personnel as hostages, some of whom were placed in key areas to deter further air-strikes. Continue to paragraph 6: Events following the air-strikes have so far resulted in about 80 dead and over 160 injured. Further, the Serbs are subjecting 325 UNPROFOR personnel to inhumane and humiliating treatment. They have closed the airport, blocked land access, cut the water and electricity supplies to Sarajevo, severely restricted UNPROFOR's movement, and continuing to flout the ultimatum. And we see a similar reference if we turn to paragraph 17. On page 7, I believe. There it is. Water and electricity supplies to Sarajevo were cut by the Serbs as of Friday afternoon. And it continues that the small amount of electricity that exists would only be sufficient for emergencies, such as government buildings and hospitals. Mr. Ambassador, is this weekly situation report an accurate reflection of the circumstances in the areas mentioned, that is, both Sarajevo and the other safe areas, in late May of 1995?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger, it does. And we had anticipated that due to these air-strikes, we felt that Serbs, Bosnian Serbs reacted in the way we anticipated, and this shows that another page has been turned in the history of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And our original peacekeeping mandate with these kinds of air-strike actions by NATO with our full agreement, we entered -- we turned a page from peacekeeping to something akin to peace enforcement, and this was done on our part with -- on the basis of very clear reflection on the consequences. And, of course, at that stage the Rapid Reaction Force was not yet in existence, so we took certain risks, but, at the same time, these actions necessitated our review and possible changes to our pre-existing mandates with regard to safe areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender 30743.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P7708, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now I just want to turn to the same issue of restrictions on humanitarian supplies in another geographic area. This Trial Chamber has received information - and that's P004 -- P00042 - regarding the food situation in Srebrenica at the beginning of July 1995, specifically a report dated 8 July 1995, that, among other things, with the present rate of delivery of convoys less than 25 percent of the needs of the population would be met, and also referring to problems with water, and more specifically referring to the fact that the UNHCR planned convoy for a week is three. However, due to the persistent refusal by the Bosnian Serb army to allow into the enclave these convoys, an average of one arrives per week. In that connection, also I wanted to show you a contemporaneous document from Srebrenica sent by Colonel Karremans - that's 65 ter 25557 - who describes in point 1 that: For some months the general situation within and around the enclave of Srebrenica is deteriorating. And concludes at the bottom of that paragraph: Being hostage of the Bosnian Serb army for over more than three months, something has to be done. And then turning to paragraph 6 specifically, on the next page, he notes that on top of that: The food situation within the enclave is getting dramatic. Within some days the warehouses will be empty. He also notes there is hardly no medical aid available throughout the enclave and that schools are closed since the shelling of Srebrenica lately. And do you understand that, Mr. Ambassador, to be a reflection of the restrictions on humanitarian aid to which the inhabitants of Srebrenica were subjected in the period preceding the military operation against -- the take-over of Srebrenica in early July?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think all these shortages of food, water, and in addition the -- I think fuel was becoming extremely short, which necessitated that our -- that the Dutch contingent had to conduct their missions on foot instead of on vehicles. And these several months, in particular, several weeks, preceding July 11th were -- and the attack itself started around July 5th or 6th, it was graduated attempts to put pressure on -- on the -- on the safe area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7709, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. The first page on the top still contains some Dutch text but apparently it's an attachment to something. Mr. Tieger, I do not insist on a translation of that. But if the parties would --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If you wish to consult with your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's why I didn't speak on behalf of the Chamber. But if anyone wants this title, part 4, attachment 24, threatening situation in Srebrenica, if you would like to have that translated then we'll hear from you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, during your direct examination by Dr. Karadzic in your previous appearance, he asked you at transcript page 37734, whether you were aware that he was pressed and the non-beneficial relationship with UNPROFOR. Do you recall that he referred in meetings with you to dissatisfaction with UNPROFOR and to his view that the relationship was non-beneficial or that UNPROFOR was in his way?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. Well, maybe the simplest way is to show you a document, 65 ter 03501. Now, this is a code cable from you to Mr. Annan dated the 14th of March, 1995, referring to meetings with Bosnian Serb officials, including Dr. Karadzic. And on the second page, at paragraph 5, you refer to his comment that the Bosnian Serbs would never accept control of the border between themselves and the Krajina Serbs, and that: "UNPROFOR would be asked to leave if our intention was to exert such control." Karadzic said: "We must ask ourselves what interest we have in keeping you here - you are here to carry out the aims of the Security Council to maintain Bosnian and Croatia within their Communist (currently recognised) borders. The aims of the Security Council are being furthered by you, while our objectives are being eroded." Now, was that a reference to or reflection of Dr. Karadzic's position that UNPROFOR's objectives or mandate was incompatible with the Bosnian Serb objectives or that in some manner he was considering the end of UNPROFOR's presence in Bosnia and the advantages it would present to the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think certainly there was an increase of more belligerent words and attitude from Bosnian Serb leadership as manifested in those remarks made by Dr. Karadzic in one of our meetings in March 1995. But by and large, I think throughout the mission we had difficulty maintaining the basic tenets of peacekeeping operations based on the consent and agreement of the parties to the conflict. On the one hand, the Bosnian government, although it accepted grudgingly our presence, what they wanted in truth was some kind of a peace enforcement. On the other hand, I'd say that Bosnian Serb party was not anxious to -- to have our presence, that -- even mere presence because of -- we were -- our mandates were helping with facilitating humanitarian assistance, on the one hand, and also facilitating the stabilisation and achievement of cease-fires. And in our -- in performing these tasks, we were basically considered hindrance to their achievement of their objectives. So we had to vacillate between two parties: One wanting more vigorous activities on our part; the other wanting minimum of our achieving our mandated tasks by the UN Security Council. We had to navigate very carefully between those two waters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document. I see we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that document is already in evidence as P2050.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's no need to decide. Mr. Akashi, we take a break of half an hour exactly. We would like to see you back after half an hour. You may follow the usher. Mr. Tieger, after the break, we will resume at three minutes past 2.00. You have until 2.30 and then you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court and Mr. Ivetic, I don't believe I'll need all that time. In fact, I'm going to say ten minutes to the max and more -- closer to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break, and -- well, in view of this message, we take a break until five minutes past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom, if my information is accurate, for the next witness there are two hours remaining for cross-examination. And then, of course, we wonder whether we would be able to conclude the evidence of that witness by tomorrow, but I don't know how much time the Defence would need, which, since there's no other witness available, as I understand well, would mean that we could then cancel the Thursday session. I leave it in the hands of the parties because it would be a pity if just for ten minutes we would have to come to court on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honours, and I'll do my best to try to complete the witness tomorrow since that's what we were planning on doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if that's possible, then, of course that's ... Welcome back, Mr. Akashi. Mr. Tieger will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, just before we adjourned, I had been asking you about some of the views of Dr. Karadzic in respect of the presence or absence of UNPROFOR in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in that connection, I wanted to call up 65 ter 02934. This is an interview with "Der Spiegel" that Dr. Karadzic gave on 29th of August, 1994. And if we turn to the second column in English and page 2 of the B/C/S translation ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have two times -- I think we now have the English translation and the B/C/S translation of what is originally in German and perhaps we might have a look at the German ourselves at this moment but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, the following passage in which Dr. Karadzic refers to, and again that's the beginning of the second half of the second column, where Dr. Karadzic refers to weapons that have not yet been used in the war, he ask is asked: "Now are you boasting, the UN commanders, above all the French, plan to withdraw from Bosnia if the latest peace initiative fails. Do you expect an escalation of the war in this case?"

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could scroll down. The English is actually not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Dr. Karadzic responds: "Then the Muslims will disappear, and we will split Bosnia up between ourselves and the Croats, because they are in great danger without us. The Muslims would devour them, and the Croats know that very well. A Croatian-Serbian pact would be the ideal solution." Dr. Karadzic is then asked: "Do you want to kill the remaining Muslims or keep them on reservations, like the American Indians?" And Dr. Karadzic responds: "We Serbs will grant them a certain autonomy around Tuzla, the Croats will do so around Zenica. But that is it." Mr. Ambassador, were you concerned that the withdrawal or neutralisation of UNPROFOR could have such dire [Realtime transcript read in error "diver"] consequences for the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any attempt on my part to exaggerate, the role UNPROFOR was playing in this most unfortunate conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think, despite all our shortcomings, UNPROFOR nevertheless played an essential role of impartial buffer and our humanitarian tasks were quite significant. We were not always given necessary means to fulfil our objectives, but we tried our best. And we were misunderstood by one -- by one party or another, or by both times -- by both parties, but I think we were not, of course, instrument in the hands of one party or another. We cannot be. And so we did our very best, and I would not pay too much attention to what Dr. Karadzic might have said at one time or another. He was sometimes quite flamboyant and sometimes quite even fanciful and boastful, and so you have to carefully balance the situation in which he spoke with the words he spoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Akashi, however, the question was whether you had concerns that the withdrawal of the --or the neutralisation of UNPROFOR would have such consequences. I don't know whether you gave that any thought --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what do you mean by "neutralisation"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's -- let's just start with the withdrawal perhaps, whether the withdrawal would have consequences, whether you were concerned that it would -- a withdrawal would have such diverse consequences for the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the answer to that question would vary according to the specific time when that question would have been raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I leave it in Mr. Tieger's hands whether he wants to follow up and ask for specific times or -- and.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you can please look at page 35, line 10, and ascertain whether the word you used was "diver" or "dire."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The word was "dire," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And thanks for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it further in your hands, Mr. Tieger, whether have you any follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do I understand you, Mr. Ambassador, to -- that you're indicating that you would measure the language used with what was happening -- the information you were getting about what was happening on the ground, with related comments, with the totality of the factors involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 02934 receives Exhibit Number P7710, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Ambassador, we had earlier discussed one aspect of your booklet referring to an assessment of Dr. Karadzic. I'd like to turn your attention now to a portion of your booklet which refers to Mr. Mladic, and that is found under -- in -- at page 43 in e-court under the heading -- the subchapter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give the document number?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. 1D04654. If we turn to page 43, please. We see this is found in a sub -- in a portion of a chapter which is entitled: "A world tinged by deep-seated grudges and revenge." Begins: "Another emotional nationalist was Ratko Mladic, Supreme Commander of Bosnian Serb forces." If I could continue on to page 44, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think the text continues on to page 44. There's parts that are being skipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page -- page 4 -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court pages are not corresponding --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with the hard copy pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The hard copy pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: E-court pages are not corresponding with the hard copy pages because there are two hard copy pages on one e-court page. Mr. Tieger, could you clearly explain from what page are you reading in e-court. Or from the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Or both, of course. We began --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In both there's more text, that's what I'm saying. In both the hard copy and the e-court there's more text. So it's incorrect to say it goes on to the next page if you don't read that text. It's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's clear that Mr. Tieger read the beginning of that paragraph. There's more on that page but he has chosen to continue to read a little bit further on the next page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm happy to tender the pages I refer to in their totality, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, that began on page 81 of the hard copy and page 43 of e-court. On page 83 of the hard copy, page 44 in e-court, your booklet states: "One could sense from Mladic's conversations his blind love for Serbs. The death of one Serbian soldier was the source of greatest sorrow to him. At one time he cited the population figure of a certain area which seemed too large. On inspection, we found out that he was counting war dead as if they were still alive. His strong feelings for the lives of Serbs did not seem to extend to the lives of other ethnic peoples in the same country." And one more passage found at page 85 of the hard copy and page 44 in e-court --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could just for the record note that this was on page 82 and not page 83 as counsel has indicated. We're having a very hard time following him reading sections when he gives wrong citations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I fully agree with that, and I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you need assistance, Mr. Ivetic, we will be glad to help you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in this instance I'm confident it's page 85 of the hard copy and page 44 of e-court at the first full paragraph. And there's a passage which provides: "At any rate, the world of General Mladic seemed to be tinged with the notion of Serb supremacy and full of deep-seated grudge and vengeance. The atrocities of Srebrenica in July 1995 may have been partly a revenge of the massacre of Serbs by Muslim soldiers in the vicinity in December 1992. The nationalist Mladic brought up in traditional Balkan culture might have acted out in the spirit of the feudal ages, characterised by endless violence and revenge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the question but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then we'll wait for the question as well. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is that an accurate reflection of the passages in your book and did that accurately reflect your view of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have an objection to the second part of the two-pronged question. The second part gives cause for speculation that we don't have the basis for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second part of the question was whether it accurately reflects the view of the witness and I have difficulties to understand how that could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It asks for the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- asking for speculation. It may be that the views of the witness, and that's apparently what he wants to draw our attention to, may be speculative. But whether or not -- the question was whether it reflects the views, speculative or not, and the answer to that question is not a matter of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, the objection is denied. And the witness is invited to answer the two-pronged question. If you want to hear it again, Mr. Tieger will put the question to you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll eliminate the first prong since I think there is probably a consensus about the first in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did that accurately reflect your views, Mr. Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you can see that these are my views, but these are speculative views on my part. I'm not a historian by profession. So I was just thinking aloud here by saying that the world of General Mladic seems -- seemed to be tinged with a notion of Serb supremacy. The atrocities of Srebrenica may have been partly a revenge, and the last sentence of that paragraph, the nationalist Mladic might have acted out in the spirit of the feudal ages. So these are all subjectives. So I'm not speaking with 100 per cent accuracy but I'm -- sort of was thinking aloud in these sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Ambassador, but just to clarify further, do I understand correctly that those views, that is, your thinking aloud in the booklet, was based upon your experiences in Bosnia and particularly your exchanges and meetings and discussions with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this -- these passages, yes, reflected, indeed, my thoughts created partly by my actual experiences of my encounters in the discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I put additional few words on my part, Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you'll be reexamined by Mr. Ivetic. If you think that it should be at this point in time, then I'll give you an opportunity to do so. If you would say: I'd rather add anything at the end of my testimony, then we'll wait until Mr. Ivetic has -- I leave it to you whether you think this is the right moment to add something to what you said before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, to dispel any doubts, I am not expressing a deterministic view in this passage or in any other passages. And in connection with Srebrenica, I'm not saying here that what happened in a sense should have happened because of a certain historical viewpoint on the part of certain people. The point is that the Srebrenica tragedy may have happened sort of on the basis of opportunistic viewpoint on the part of the Bosnian Serb military leadership. They may not have planned to conquer the entire area, but having seen the relative weakness of the opposing side and relative mildness of the firmness with which the enclave was held by the UN troops, the -- the Bosnian Serb party may have been emboldened on the basis of evolving situation to do more than they had initially attempted. Am I clear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you are expressing, which you did you before, that you have not determined or established anything with certainty but, as you wrote in your book, that you have given it some thoughts of what may have happened, and you're now further explaining what may have been the case. Now, this Chamber is tasked with establishing, to the extent relevant for our judgement, to establish what did happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me, as I indicated I would do when I was asking the questions in respect of that portion of the booklet, I would tender or ask that pages 43 through 45 be added --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will be added to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Ivetic, when you were consulting with Mr. Mladic, Mr. Tieger said to the Chamber that he would like to add the portions he just dealt with to the excerpts he intends to tender -- he wants to tender. I'm just drawing your attention to it, that that's what happened. Do you have any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Akashi, Mr. Ivetic will now put further questions to you in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Ambassador. During cross-examination, you were asked about P631, which I'd like to call up in e-court, and this was at transcript page 41746 where Mr. Tieger asked you about the language about inter-disposition of UNPROFOR. So I want to take a look at that document which we have on our screens. And I'd like to focus on the third paragraph, the second half of that paragraph, which reads as follows: "Rather than entering into any written agreement, UNPROFOR only noted their concerns and gave assurances that UNPROFOR units would be interpositioned between the two sides along confrontation lines. The Bosnian Serb side nevertheless reserved its right to take adequate measures of self-defence in case of attack by the other side. We did not endorse their position." And the question I wanted to ask you: If I am understanding this document and your testimony yesterday correctly, these assurances of interpositioning forces by UNPROFOR were meant to address the Serb concerns about being attacked. Am I right in that understanding?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then the question I have is what was supposed to happen if UNPROFOR could not succeed in interpositioning itself between the ABiH and the VRS at the confrontation line as had been assured?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you reiterate your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. What was supposed to happen if UNPROFOR could not succeed in interpositioning itself between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serb side at the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But UNPROFOR was interpositioned. What -- what was disputed between the parties, two parties, was how many UNPROFOR troops should be interpositioned at weapons collection points. And we wanted the number of troops sufficient to do the job of interpositioning, but if these points under the control of UNPROFOR troops were attacked by one of the two parties with a strength beyond UNPROFOR's capability, then we would not be able to do the job. Am I -- do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do, sir, and I'd like now to look at D112 again, which was the 16 August 1994 cable from yourself to Mr. Annan that we looked at earlier that initially had sent a copy of the protocol which the document we just looked at said had not been signed. And in relation to this document, I'd like to turn to page 2 and focus on item number 4, which states: "The fundamental question, however, revolves around the potential demand by the BSA to use weapons from the WCP in the Sarajevo EZ, under the right of self-defence. While the UNPROFOR reaction in general would be to deal with the Serb's concerns [sic] by negotiating and interpositioning, this may not dissuade BSA action. Moreover, the BiH has repeatedly opposed the interpositioning of UNPROFOR troops, particularly on the Visoko-Olovo front." The first question I have for you, sir: Does this document accurately reflect the condition on the ground that during the time-period in August of 1994 during this fighting the BiH was opposing the interpositioning of UNPROFOR between itself and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm afraid I will not be able to give you a clear-cut answer because the notion of self-defence can be interpreted by different parties differently. There are innumerable instances in all kinds of other conflicts in which one party or another has interpreted its right of self-defence in a distorted or exaggerated manner. In other cases, maybe exercise of the right of self-defence, it is entirely justifiable. So as to which interpretation applies to this particular case is beyond my capacity and it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. And, sir, that's why I'm asking you about the text in your cable which claims that the BiH has repeatedly opposed the interpositioning of UNPROFOR troops and asking you if this was, in fact, the situation during this time-period, that interpositioning was not made possible by the BiH side, that is, the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That builds something into the question that is clearly not contained in the document that the -- the documents referred to opposition by the BiH and now Mr. Ivetic has transformed that to making it impossible. Seems like quite different things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Ivetic, rephrase the questioning with a question because there are a few things implied in your question which do not appear from the text. And as a re-examining party, I think the first thing we'd have to do is to find out what is really said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would then go back to my original question which I asked at page 44, line 23, which was: Does this document accurately reflect the condition on the ground that during the time-period in August of 1994 during this fighting the BiH was opposing the interpositioning of UNPROFOR between itself and the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's more or less what the text says. But if -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to bring the attention of this Chamber to paragraph 6 of the document in question, in which I, in this case, myself, have brought the concerns expressed in your Z-2571 to General Rose's attention, with my own personal request for restraint in his public statements. And I may encourage -- I also encourage him to seek political advice in the drafting of sensitive written communications. This kind of admonition is quite rare. And so I think these matters should be -- should be considered in the context of the conditions of discussion taking place in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. I nevertheless would still have a question. And now focusing again on paragraph 4, where it reads: "Moreover, the BiH has repeatedly opposed the interpositioning of UNPROFOR troops, particularly on the Visoko-Olovo front." If you know, could you tell us whether UNPROFOR troops were already interpositioned when BiH opposed to that or were they not yet interpositioned? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
