utterances.text: In this case, I do not know. But UNPROFOR normally negotiates in good faith with the two parties, and when we felt interpositioning is indeed justified, then we interposed ourselves. And if not, no interposition would take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a little point of clarification. Do you interpose yourselves notwithstanding any opposition from either or both parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said: In this case, I do not know. But UNPROFOR normally interpositioned is indeed justified, then the inter -- then we interpose ourselves. Now when you interpose yourself, my question is: Do you do that notwithstanding any opposition from either party or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually we do interpose ourselves on the basis of agreement or consent by two parties. In that case, only minimum presence of UNPROFOR will be needed. But I think we interpose when we honestly feel that it is required to assuage the tension and obviate the possibility of military confrontation. In case we do it, in the circumstances of one or the other party having serious reservation or objection, then our strength has to be greater than otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, you have raised paragraph 6 of this same document calling for restraint on the part of General Rose in his public statements. What were the concerns as to General Rose's public statements such that he needed restraint?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know in this particular instance what were the remarks on the part of General Michael Rose which occasioned this comment. But General Rose was always very quick in action, which I appreciated, and, you know, he had experiences of special forces in the Falkland/Malvinas situation, and I appreciated his very assertive, quick action, with a few exceptions in which I would have preferred more cautious, more meditated action based on consultation with us at UNPROFOR headquarters. So I already referred yesterday to confusion between close air support and air-strike on the part of military senior staff. That's one instance in which the military people may not be at all instances cognizant of political implications of the words, terms, used. So all these -- the UNPROFOR was always based on a collective decision combining the civilian judgement with military advice. So always we tried to stand on our collective judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you were asked about the claim that this protocol which is an attached to this cable was drafted by the Serb side, and that was at transcript page 41746. I'd like to turn to page 4 with you and to look at that document, and I think you will note here that the Serb side is constantly referred to by the acronym BSA. What was the official way that the Serb side referred to their army in other documents they drafted? Was it BSA or something else?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When documents from the Serb side were received by the UN, would they normally be written in English or in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally in English for our perusal by the top leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would those communications be signed or unsigned?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go back to page 1 of the cable, so page 1 of this document, and we see here that the cable uses the acronym BSA to refer to the Serb side. Was that typical for how UN documents referred to the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in our communication in the theatre as such or in our communication between -- between Zagreb and New York, we may use this terminology, including BSA. But if it becomes a document to be sent to the Security Council, we have to be much more formal and the terminology has to be based on the common diplomatic usage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if we just briefly go back to P631 for one more thing which is to be found on page 3 of the same and this will be the analysis of the legal advisor as to the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's paragraph 7 on that page. I think we have ... is this P631? In both languages? I see on the B/C/S it appears to be. The English appears to be a different document. And if we can go to page 3 and focus on part 7 in both languages. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the first part says: "That, in a particular scenario, the BSA forces might or might not have a right of self-defence." And the footnote says: "I point out that such a right could not flow from Article 51 of the Charter since the Bosnian Serb party is not a state or a member of the United Nations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To see the footnote. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Such a right would therefore have to arise from some other source, e.g., customary law." And the question I have for you, sir: Am I to understand that the UN legal advisor is espousing the view that the right to self-defence only applies to members of the UN?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's certainly not what the footnotes says or even suggests. It -- Mr. Ivetic, so where if you asked this question, could you please then pay better attention to footnote 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours. And I'm paying to the text of paragraph 7 which says "might not." So I believe the question is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says: "It could not flow from Article 51 of the Charter," so that's one source, whereas further down it refers to possible other sources. And that's, I think, the issue which in your question was neglected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a jurist, but Article 51 of the UN Charter refers to the inherent right of individual and collective self-defence and I think it's couched in a specific context, and I think for us to extract any words out of Article 51 is rather precarious.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I interrupted Mr. Ivetic when he was phrasing a question. Now, you've given an answer without even knowing exactly what the question would be. Mr. Ivetic, I don't want to deprive you of your right to question the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've had some evidence in this courtroom by at least two witnesses citing to Article 60 of the Geneva Conventions and the right of self-defence in that instance. Do you believe that that would apply to the situation as discussed in this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's very fair -- I mean, I leave it to the witness, but he just got finished saying he is not a jurist and he seems to be asked for that type of opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I leave it to the witness to -- to ask you to present to him any text which is part of your question or whether he can answer the question without consulting such a text. And ... Mr. Akashi, therefore, you're invited to answer the question as you deem fit. Or let me just see ... it's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can rephrase the question, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was Article 60 of the Geneva Conventions an item discussed within the UN prior to the drafting of this document that was then sent by yourself to the UN in New York?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Article 60 of all the Geneva Conventions, is that the same? I mean, I know of at least the four major conventions of Geneva, and if Article 60 of all of them is the same, then -- but I would have to check that. Have you checked it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I haven't. And I think depending on the answer of the witness, was the right of self-defence under the Geneva Conventions discussed and taken into account prior to the drafting of this document, the witness can either say it was. I don't know what article it was or he doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is certainly able to phrase an answer, so what he could say, we leave that in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we leave that to him and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a recollection whether the discussion of Geneva Conventions, et cetera, took place in preparation of this cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Then I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 1D3055 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What we have is dated 21st of February, 1994, from yourself to Mr. Annan and it references meetings with Dr. Karadzic and President Izetbegovic. And I'd like to turn to page 3 and look at paragraph number 6: "On the issue of self-defence, General Rose noted that it would not be possible for the Muslims to attack Serb regrouping centres due to the presence of UNPROFOR at such sites. However, in the event of such an action, UNPROFOR would provide the first line of defence, but it was also understood that if the Serbs wished to withdraw their weapons, for example, in the face of a massive attack, there was nothing UNPROFOR could do to stop them. It was hoped that such an eventuality would not occur as it would indicate a total breakdown of the peace process in Sarajevo." Does this document accurately reflect the negotiations as to the exercise of self-defence in relation to the weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th of February was a rather crucial date. This is two days prior to the deadline for the NATO ultimatum for air-strike over the Sarajevo safe area in the event of no withdrawal of Bosnian Serb weapons from the exclusion zone of 20 kilometres from the centre of Sarajevo. And I remember we were anxiously watching every step which each of the two parties take in fulfilment of the requirements for not activating a NATO air-strike. And we were mostly in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Mladic reduce the volume of his voice when he consults with counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we were watching the situation mostly from Zagreb but in close consultation with our -- also Sarajevo headquarters. And so in that sense, we were watching everything we ourselves do as well as what the parties do, and we were also consulting closely with NATO and, of course, with the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could turn to the next page, and if we can look at paragraph 15 at the bottom of the page which will then go on to the next page, it says: "The meeting ended with UNPROFOR presenting an oral draft protocol on the agreements reached at the meeting. The protocol contained the following three points ..." And then we have the points that I think were the Weapons Collection Agreement. And then in item number 1, in the meeting with President Izetbegovic, it said: "Mr. Akashi briefed President Izetbegovic on his meeting with Dr. Karadzic, noting that the main emphasis of his talks had been on the need to take full advantage of the momentum for peace in Sarajevo. While a lot of details still remained to be discussed, Dr. Karadzic had agreed that verification and control procedures by UNPROFOR should start at noon the following day. He had also agreed to try to withdraw and regroup Serb weapons by 2400 hours of 19 February 1994." Ambassador, the -- a lot of details that remained to be discussed, was the right to self-defence and a response to an ABiH attack that could not be stopped one of those details remaining to be discussed after the Serbs had agreed to the weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection of discussions around 18th and 19th of February, 1994, what concerned me most was a question of remaining weapons within the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. And I was very happy, I remember, that general -- the Admiral Boorda of NATO southern command and our generals, General de Lapresle, at my headquarters in Zagreb, and -- were of the same opinion, that because of the heavy snow, not all Serb weapons were withdrawn from that exclusion zone but we had our troops controlling those remaining weapons within the zone. And Admiral Boorda was in agreement with us. Therefore we were satisfied that substantial party of those weapons had been withdrawn. The remaining weapons were under our supervision and control. Therefore there was no reason to think that NATO ultimatum was still unfulfilled. I like that pragmatic approach taken by our military with full consent of NATO southern command. So on both sides there's not total insistence on every letter of the ultimatum, and so UNPROFOR had obligation to make sure that even those weapons which are yet to be withdrawn should be under our full control. So there was a degree of good faith involved, and under the circumstances, there was a good sense of pragmatism on all parties engaged in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the document, 1D3055.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives Exhibit Number D1364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you were cross-examined extensively about Gorazde so I will have some questions for you on that topic. And I'd like to first call up D1362 of which I believe page 3 was shown to you during the cross-examination at transcript page 41758. And so I'd like to turn to page 3 of that document and I'd like to focus on the middle of paragraph number 4 which starts off: "Continuing, Mr. Akashi said that there should be no illusions on any side of the seriousness of the present situation and of the international community's revulsion towards it. Thus, while the general issue of safe areas could and would be addressed in the near future, the immediate concern was the human and humanitarian tragedy in Gorazde, a tragedy out of proportion to any provocation that the BSA may have initially had from the BiH." And then reference is also made to the unacceptably high civilian casualties of the previous day, 100. The question I have: This promise that the general issue of the safe areas would be addressed in the near future, was it addressed in the near future, following this document dated 23 April 1994 resulting from the marathon negotiations you had, I believe, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that UN Secretary-General presented to the Security Council at certain frequency his review and his reflections on how the safe area regime should be revised or rectified or improved. And I think -- I cannot say when specifically, but soon after this Gorazde crisis, one such review was sent to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the casualties from Gorazde, I think in yesterday's transcript at 41754 you said you had relied upon UNMOs and others as to information about Gorazde. Were you aware of any complaints as to the unreliability of reporting from Gorazde, specifically the Bosnian government and UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I think there was a high degree of reliability on the reports which we received from UNMOs in the Gorazde area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to first take a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, if we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn to P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm also looking at the clock. I think the time you announced you'd still need, you went beyond that. We have to stop at 3.30. I don't know whether Mr. Tieger has any further questions for the witness. Not at this moment. So please keep in mind that we have to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I know, and we took half an hour instead of five minutes at the beginning for the Prosecution's questions. I have approximately 13 more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then we have a -- we'll check. I think, as a matter of fact, that Mr. Tieger stayed well within his time, even took shorter time than he asked for and what was granted and that it's -- I said in view of Mr. Tieger's answer I would even grant two additional minutes before we would resume after the break. Mr. Tieger, I think, stayed well within his half-hour and it's you who took far more than the 40 minutes you announced --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Tieger announced five minutes -- ten minutes, closer to five minutes. That was just before the last break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was entitled to another half an hour, Mr. Ivetic. And he may have taken a little bit more than his reduced assessment, but you're invited to finish within the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to P736, page 25, in the English. I think for our purposes, since it is a large document, we can look at the English and since I'll be reading it we'll get the translation. This is the statement of General Rose to the Prosecutor of the Tribunal introduced as evidence and if we could look at paragraph number 103: "On 12 May 1994, I visited Gorazde. I met with the chief UNMO who had been responsible for some of the inaccurate reporting from Gorazde. I told him that misleading reports had done great damage to the credibility of the UN mission. The inaccuracy of the UNMO reports was demonstrated by my visit to the hospital. The UNMOs had specifically stated that the hospital had been targeted throughout the day with tanks, wire-guided missiles, and indirect fire with the aim of destroying it. Yet the director of the hospital, Dr. Begovic, told me that although a shell had landed in a house nearby, killing a number of patients sheltering there, the hospital itself had only been hit twice: Once in a stairwell and once in an empty room on the top floor."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Does this accord with your information that was available to you as to Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already told the Chamber, there was a shortage or distortion in some of the information we were receiving from Gorazde, and we were trying our best to have access to accurate and up-to-date information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And looking at the last part of paragraph 102 of General Rose's statement, he says: "Yet neither the final casualty list, heavy though it was, nor the relatively undamaged state of the buildings in the town suggested that the Serbs had systematically targeted civilians." Would you agree that the situation encountered by the UN when entering Gorazde was less dire than had been proclaimed in the time-period leading up to the actions to be taken against the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That conflates a lot of information, I'm afraid, and Mr. Ivetic indicated that himself. There is information coming from different sources. So when you say the information that was proclaimed, it is impossible to know whether he's talking about information from one source or the other, or the sources the witness relied or -- et cetera. It -- it creates a potentially -- or asks for a potentially misleading response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe in the cross-examination Mr. Tieger used a document that described the situation as dire. I can't find the reference right now obviously on my feet, but it was today, after I gave my estimate of time, when we had another hour and a half of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, my reference to "dire" was in connection with the last document in the Karadzic interview and what would happen with -- if UNPROFOR left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it's a ... If the witness an is able to answer the question, he may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, it was read to you part of the statement and the question was whether you agree that situation encountered by the UN, I think, entering Gorazde was -- perhaps you rephrase it, because it doesn't appear that clearly in the transcript, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with -- let me rephrase it entirely. Would you agree with General Rose that the situation encountered by the UN when entering Gorazde did not suggest that the Serbs had systematically targeted civilians?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would agree with every word used by General Rose, because I know some other sources felt that General Rose was underestimating, while he may have been right that the other side was exaggerating. So like so many instances, maybe the truth is somewhere in the middle, among these confusing figures and assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at D186 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, it is dated the 18th of April, 1994, and is addressed to yourself and it comes from Viktor Andreev who I believe was your deputy. And if we can go to page 2 --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, no, he was not my deputy but deputy to Sergio de Mello.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I apologise. And if we could turn to the second page and paragraph 10, this is imploring that the Security Council must clarify the concept of safe areas as soon as possible. And I think the same type of complaints that you discussed yesterday are listed in here. And I would like to then turn to the next page, which is the last page in this document and it states at 11: "UNPROFOR's mandate has pushed it into low-level conflict with the Serbs. As a result, Sarajevo is blockaded, its airport is closed, food stocks are declining. Our mandate must either be one within which we are able to have a co-operative relationship with the Serbs, or it must be one in which we have the force to impose our will. It cannot be - as it is now - somewhere in between." First of all, do you agree that by this point in time UNPROFOR was in a low-level conflict with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I -- I agree with every word used by my former colleague, Viktor Andreev, because sometimes our relationship with the Bosnian Serbs was lower than lower level and sometimes higher. It varied from situation to situation, and changed from location to location. It was a dynamic, changing relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at D1356, which is dated August 10, 1995, from General Janvier to Mr. Annan, and if we could turn to page 7 of the same we have a letter from General Janvier to Admiral and on the last page we see it's Admiral Layton Smith. And if we look at the third paragraph: "An intervention as contemplated will lead to perception by the party affected that NATO and the UN have declared war on it. Freedom of movement through the territory controlled by that party will end. UN troops will have become a party to the conflict, and enclaves as well as other isolated locations will be neither resupplied nor rotated using land routes. Resupply and rotation will have to be by air, which will be subjected to hostile fire. Hostages will be taken again, are likely to be treated as prisoners of war and used as human shields. Most UNPROFOR camps are within range of mortar and artillery fire, and are likely to be targeted by the party concerned." Ambassador, is General Janvier describing the situation ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is General Janvier accurately describing the effect of initiating air action against the Serb side in your understanding of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If we scroll up, we'll see that this is on the letterhead of Lieutenant-General Bernard Janvier --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1995, yeah.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Janvier, yes. Not de Lapresle, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. So now do you agree, is General Janvier accurately describing the effect of initiating air action against the Serb side in your understanding of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Janvier was in full agreement with me with regard to the two air-strikes in the month of May 1995. Now he's confronting another situation of a much more dramatic, much more massive air-strike possibility, which actually took place in the latter part of August. And I think it was a dramatic situation. I don't think General Janvier was exaggerating. It -- that air-strike was a sustained one for the first time. It lasted for about a week and then suspended briefly, then resumed a few more days, but eventually it led to the sustained period of truce. So one has to weigh the dire possibility of worsening of the situation involving our own position in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the -- the diplomatic stake which was considered worth while to take. So I think in hindsight, maybe it was a risk one had to take. But we were very apprehensive of dire consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I said you have until 25 minutes to 4.00. It's now 20 minutes to 4.00 so I -- you have to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, then I want it on the record that the Defence has not been permitted to finish its redirect examination due to the technical problems that were beyond the control of the Defence that did not enable this Court to sit the entire session today. And that we're not being entitled to a full opportunity given that my estimate was given before listening to one hour and 50 minutes of additional

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, didn't you ask earlier for 40 minutes today?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No Your Honours, I estimated approximately 40 minutes before Mr. Tieger started one hour and 50 minutes of additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you gave your assessment in saying that it would then -- that you would need more. Usually we always invite the parties to give an assessment of what they need at the end of the other party having concluded its testimony [sic]. Because you've now taken -- if it is -- I think, as a matter of fact, Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Mladic makes a sign that he wants to consult with you. Could you please -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My client has communicated that he is agreeable to continue so long as he is given approximately ten minutes to take a bathroom break in the quest of completing this witness, and I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a problem there. Because, first of all, those who are assisting us cannot go on forever. That's one. We have asked for an extended session. As a matter of fact, to say that today we couldn't finish because of the technical difficulties, everyone expected this morning that we would conclude to hear the testimony of Mr. Akashi and then continue with Mr. Kovac. So I don't think that the Chamber can agree with your position in that respect. How much time actually you would still need -- and apart from that, there are other commitments as well. I already postponed some of them. And the tapes also do not allow us to continue forever. They have to be changed anyhow. How much time would you still need, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes at a minimum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I mean, ten minutes. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a minimum, Mr. Ivetic, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I meant to say ten minutes I'll make use of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At a maximum?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If interpreters and all others assisting us would be willing to work on for another ten minutes, it couldn't be very much beyond that because the tape is ending anyhow in two hours. Mr. Tieger, any problem? As matters stand now any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, still no more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Still no more questions. Mr. Ivetic, it is exactly now quarter to 4.00. You may continue until five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at P7708 which was shown by the Prosecution in cross-examination today, and I'd like to turn to paragraph number 3 which should be on page 3 -- or page 2, I apologise. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we can have General Mladic attend to the bathroom, we have his consent to proceed in his absence to comply with the ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Mladic, if he waives his right to be present for those few minutes, then we'll continue. And, of course, you are allowed to go to the bathroom, Mr. Mladic. Yes, you may follow the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. Mladic waved his head "yes" in waiving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. You have until four minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: At paragraph 3, it says that: "Karadzic cited UN impotence in Western Slavonia and warned that UNPROFOR would be treated as an enemy if Serb positions were attacked from the air." Isn't that consistent with all the communications with the Serb side as to how they regarded the enforcement of both close air support and NATO strikes at the request of the UN?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not share the view of Mr. Ivetic [sic] with regard to the air action by NATO, which usually is co-ordinated with UNPROFOR, and although Bosnian Serbs sometimes confused close air support with the air-strikes, I think in truth they were aware of very significant difference between the two kinds of air action. And it is only air-strike which could be massive in scale and quite far-reaching in consequence, which created a lot of concern on the part of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Was the message conveyed by Bosnian Serb negotiators consistent with what is written on the screen in a UN report that Karadzic warned: We will consider you the enemy?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic excelled in dramatic words, and so we did not always believe in face value what his careful expressions might in fact mean.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Yesterday at transcript page 41741, you were asked about a portion of your book -- booklet, pardon me, 1D4654, page 15, which is pages 26 and 27 of the underlying booklet, where you cited General Michael Rose saying: "Although all three sides were to some extent guilty of war crimes, genocide did not form part of official Bosnian government policy in the way that it clearly did with the Serbs. Nevertheless, the Bosnian Serbs were not the sole perpetrators of atrocities and this fact was difficult to communicate to the members of the international community." Do you happen to know when General Rose made those comments?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. And do you agree 100 per cent with his comments?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. That's what I thought, but I wanted to make it clear. We have had at this trial evidence that the ABiH side -- and this is from transcript page 32394 and through 32396. It was in open session. It was a member of the Commission for Exchange of Prisoners of War, Mr. Krcmar, talking about a situation where Mujahedin in Maglic, Teslic, and Tesanj had decapitated several captured Bosnian Serb prisoners and were displaying their severed heads in a videotape. Did you have knowledge of the actions of Mujahedin within the ABiH of that nature?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific instance which you yourself, Mr. Ivetic, cited was entire news to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And if we can turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe I raised that and I'm curious about the -- the pleading for time and then turning to a subject that does not seem to have been addressed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Look at the part that you cited from General Rose. That's precisely the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it is or not, the witness has answered the question. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can look at P7700, which was used by Mr. Tieger earlier today. P7700. Or if it is easier that was 65 ter 31392. If we can look at page 2 in the English, page 1 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And we're looking at paragraph 1.5 which was shown to you by Mr. Tieger. And it talks about soldiers who had fled Smoluca, Potpec, and Tinja. Do you know what happened to these villages listed here, Smoluca, Potpec, and Tinja, prior to October 1994, the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you addressing me?

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And lastly, as to General Mladic, on how many occasions did you have occasion to meet with General Mladic so as to form the -- just how many times did you meet with General Mladic, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with General Mladic usually and in most instances together with the other leaders of Bosnian Serbs, Dr. Karadzic and some others, Koljevic, Krajisnik, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, sorry to interrupt you, but Mr. Ivetic is under a time restraint. Could you tell us approximately how many times you met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not count, but probably 15 times to 20 times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And on those times were you primarily talking with General Mladic or with other persons present for the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke mostly with Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: And so what portion of that time during those ten, 15, 20 meetings was spent talking directly with General Mladic, 50 per cent, 25 percent, 90 per cent, any approximation?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 25 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTION
utterances.text: Okay. Ambassador, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thank everyone for the additional time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you even stayed one minute within the time because we moved it from five minutes to 4.00 to four minutes to 4.00. Mr. Tieger -- I mean, within the time granted. Mr. Tieger, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think I have one question in clarification, Mr. President. Just one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, today you were re-directed to the passage in your booklet about General Rose's comments, so you talked about that before. Today you told Mr. Ivetic you didn't agree - let me see where I find that - 100 per cent with General Rose's comments. Yesterday the Court directed your attention to that particular passage that you included in your book about General Rose's reference to the Bosnian Serb policy and you noted that although you didn't agree with General Rose on all matters, and more frequently were in accord with Mr. Owen, that with respect to that paragraph you were in agreement. So I just wanted to clarify. Is it the case that with respect to that particular paragraph, that is, that although all three sides were to some extent guilty of war crimes, war crimes, genocide, those did not form part of official Bosnian government policy in the way that it clearly did with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in that particular paragraph General went -- General Rose went a little bit beyond his depth and -- but I said I'm in general agreement on the rather wide distribution of instances of crimes or atrocities between the two parties in the -- in conflict. And I think Lord Owen was perhaps more precise than General Rose, although they are jumbled together in the same paragraph. But as I indicated, I do not agree with every word which is said in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's about all the time I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Akashi, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and questions put to you by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [ Thank you very much, Mr. President. You were very generous and gracious, and I hope that my remarks have been of some use for your difficult task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those words. I wish you a safe return home again. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with all technicalities at a later stage including any redaction of associated exhibits, Mr. Ivetic. As far as if you could ever assist the Chamber in pointing at an Article 60 which deals with self-defence, then that might add to the sources the Chamber can rely upon because paragraph 51 of the UN Charter deals exclusively with attacks on member states and the right of self-defence of member states. Apart from all that, we adjourn for the day. And I thank all those who have about been so flexible, including Mr. Mladic, for enabling us to conclude the testimony of this witness today. And we resume tomorrow, the 25th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
